clue.text: See 24
See 11
Ball on head to turn cup tie

indicators.note: to turn tells us the word for cup is read backwards

parts.note: a pot is a cup, as in a trophy
a knot ties things together

explanation.surface: A football commentator describes a cup tie turning, with a ball meeting a player's head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to turn' is the reversal signal; 'Ball' is a hair bun, not a football.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairstyle with the hair gathered into a round bun on the crown of the head.

clue.text: Out on the town: certain half of Belgians drunk

indicators.note: drunk suggests the letters stagger about into a new order
half of takes the first four of the eight letters of Belgians

explanation.surface: Some of the Belgian fans are drunk, as you might expect of supporters out on the town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half of' gives BELG, the first half of Belgians; 'drunk' rearranges CERTAIN plus BELG.
explanation.definitionFit: Being out on the town means partying, marking an occasion with festivities.

clue.text: Stop longer than away supporter

parts.note: away from home means out
a stay is a prop or brace that supports something

explanation.surface: An away fan lingers in the stadium longer than the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To remain somewhere beyond the expected time, as in overstaying a welcome.

clue.text: Stand extra time? Add time on

parts.note: ET is the standard abbreviation for extra time in football
an age is a period of time
re means on, about, concerning

explanation.surface: A referee asks whether extra time should be played and adds stoppage time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Add' just strings the pieces together.
explanation.definitionFit: A French term for a piece of furniture with open shelves, a display stand for ornaments.

clue.text: See 20
Used to be what in Germany?

definitions.meaning: past tense of the verb be, as in it existed before
the German interrogative pronoun for what

explanation.surface: Someone asks what Germany once was in the football world.
explanation.definitionFit: The simple past singular of be, and also the German word asking what.

clue.text: First home international to divide most of country

parts.note: in means at home

indicators.note: to divide means the letter for international goes into the middle of the country
most of drops the final letter of the country

parts.note: Italy is a country

explanation.surface: A home international match is said to split most of a football-mad nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' drops the country's last letter; 'to divide' sends the international letter into what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: Initial means coming at the start, the opening item in a sequence.

clue.text: Equalises against Spain — topless men drink outside

indicators.note: outside says the trimmed men go round the letters for against and Spain
topless removes the top letter of men, its first in a down clue

parts.note: men taken as written before trimming
V for versus means against
E is the international vehicle code for Spain
to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: A team equalises against Spain while shirtless male fans drink outside the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' gives EN; 'outside' wraps EN round VE, making EVEN, then SUP follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To even things up is to make the score level, the same as equalising.

clue.text: Urge forward — without a goal, player doesn't finish

indicators.note: without tells us to take the letter a away from the goal word

parts.note: an aim is a goal

indicators.note: doesn't finish removes the last letter of the player's name

parts.note: Pele, the Brazilian footballer

explanation.surface: A footballer who has no goals and fails to finish chances is urged on by the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' drops A from AIM, giving IM; 'doesn't finish' cuts PELE to PEL.
explanation.definitionFit: To impel is to drive or push someone onward.

clue.text: Happen to bring up Italy going top

indicators.note: going means the letter for Italy leaves the word for bringing up

parts.note: to train is to raise or rear someone
I is the international vehicle code for Italy
a spire is the pointed top of a church tower

explanation.surface: A coach wants to bring Italy up to the top of the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going' takes I out of TRAIN, leaving TRAN; 'top' is a noun here, not Italy rising.
explanation.definitionFit: Transpire is commonly used to mean occur or come about.

clue.text: Breaking one's heart, 1-0, England out

indicators.note: breaking suggests the letters are smashed and reassembled
the heart of one is its middle letter

parts.note: the figure 1 resembles the letter I and 0 the letter O
England taken as written

explanation.surface: A heartbreaking one-nil defeat knocks England out of the tournament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking' rearranges N (one's heart), I and O (1-0) and ENGLAND; 'out' is the definition, not a further instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Something out of line is not in alignment with the rest.

clue.text: See 20
Struggle to stop cross going over head, showing audacity

indicators.note: going over places the first part above the next in this down clue
to stop means the struggle word plugs the gap in the cross word

parts.note: to ford is to cross a river
war is a struggle
a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: A defender struggles to stop a cross going over a teammate's head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to stop' is the containment signal; 'going over' places the first part above the headland in the down entry. 'cross' is a verb, not a football pass.
explanation.definitionFit: Forwardness means boldness or presumption, a willingness to push oneself forward.

clue.text: Plant penning a new song

indicators.note: penning means the song encloses the other letters as in a pen

parts.note: a ditty is a simple song

explanation.surface: A songwriter is writing a new song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penning' looks like writing, but it means enclosing: A and N go inside DITTY.
explanation.definitionFit: An aromatic herb of the mint family, a type of flowering plant.

clue.text: Feature for cap? Shortly get wag

indicators.note: shortly means the word for get is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: to earn is to get money
to flap is to wag back and forth

explanation.surface: A footballer's partner receives an England cap quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: WAG is British slang for a footballer's wife or girlfriend, but here it is the verb. 'Shortly' cuts EARN to EAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A flap on a hat that folds down to cover the ears, a feature of some caps.

clue.text: Shot one under keeper's back with pass attempt blocked

indicators.note: blocked means the attempt word is filled by the other letters

parts.note: a bid is an attempt

indicators.note: back takes the final letter of the word

parts.note: to die is to pass away

explanation.surface: A goalkeeper's back is turned as a pass attempt is blocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' picks the final letter of keeper; 'blocked' fills the attempt word. Golf's birdie, not football, supplies the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf, a birdie is a score one under par for a hole.

clue.text: Bird with Chelsea player? John initially?

parts.note: Chelsea FC play in blue and are nicknamed the Blues
John's first letter is J, whose spoken name is spelt jay

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a bird is linked with a Chelsea player called John.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter J is written out as its name, JAY.
explanation.definitionFit: A North American crested songbird with bright blue plumage.

clue.text: Stage to run out and play

parts.note: RO is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for run out
to strum is to play a guitar

explanation.surface: A performer goes on stage, runs out and plays.
explanation.walkthrough: RO is how a cricket scorecard records a batter run out.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised platform for a speaker or conductor, a small stage.

clue.text: Stones handled by him? Caught one in fight

indicators.note: caught as in heard, so the word that follows is spoken aloud

parts.note: someone who handles precious stones is a gem dealer, a jeweller

explanation.surface: Defender John Stones handled the ball and was caught by a player in a scrap.
explanation.walkthrough: John Stones is an England footballer; the stones here are gems. Some solvers find the two words a loose sound match.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who fights a duel is a combatant in a formal fight.

clue.text: Description of tree in farm next to fences?

indicators.note: fences means the next-to word encloses the farm word

parts.note: by means next to, beside
a ranch is a large farm

explanation.surface: Someone describes a tree standing in a farm beside its fences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fences' is a verb meaning encloses, not the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective for a tree with many limbs spreading out.

clue.text: Go over to fellow player

indicators.note: over in a down clue means the go word is turned upwards

parts.note: a stab is a go, an attempt
a man is a fellow

explanation.surface: A footballer goes over to a teammate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' is the reversal signal; the player turns out to be a cricketer, not a footballer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricketer who bats is a player in the team.

clue.text: Be sub twice — Gareth Bale fit to swap wingers?

indicators.note: to swap suggests the letters trade places to form new words

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; Gareth Bale is a Welsh footballer, known as a winger

explanation.surface: Gareth Bale, now fit, is twice a substitute as the manager switches his wide men.
explanation.walkthrough: Wingers in football are wide players; here they are creatures with wings.
explanation.definitionFit: These common pale garden insects fly on wings, so they are playfully called wingers.

clue.text: Beginning? Ready to get knocked out?

indicators.note: knocked out suggests the letters are battered into a different shape

explanation.surface: A boxer asks if he is ready to be knocked out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'since the year dot' is a British idiom for since time began.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for the earliest time imaginable, the very start.

clue.text: In one section, needs nutmeg for cooking

indicators.note: for cooking suggests the ingredients are mixed up

explanation.surface: A recipe in one part of a cookbook requires nutmeg.
explanation.walkthrough: In football a nutmeg is passing the ball through an opponent's legs, a hint at the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not divided into parts stays as a single piece.

clue.text: Supporter of national side, not half

indicators.note: not half removes the back half of the side's name

parts.note: Brazil is a national football team

explanation.surface: A fan of a national team supports only half-heartedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not half' drops ZIL from BRAZIL.
explanation.definitionFit: An undergarment that supports the bust is a supporter.

clue.text: Cruel: Joe Hart makes one silly bloomer

indicators.note: silly suggests the letters are jumbled foolishly

parts.note: taken as written; Joe Hart is an England goalkeeper
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: England goalkeeper Joe Hart cruelly makes a silly error.
explanation.walkthrough: A bloomer is British slang for a blunder, the surface sense; here it means a flowering plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A type of sunflower grown for its tubers, a plant that blooms.

clue.text: Not very old England manager making money abroad

indicators.note: not means the very letter is left out

parts.note: Sven-Goran Eriksson managed England's football team

explanation.surface: A former England manager earns money overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not very' tells us to drop V from SVEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A small coin of Japan and other Asian countries, foreign currency.

clue.text: Being from Africa, wanting English win

parts.note: to land a prize is to win it

explanation.surface: An African team wants England to win.
explanation.definitionFit: An antelope native to Africa, a living creature from that continent.

clue.text: Nation to watch players, missing start

indicators.note: missing start removes the first letter of the combined words

parts.note: to eye is to watch
men are players in a team

explanation.surface: A nation comes to watch its players, who miss the kick-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing start' drops the first E of EYEMEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A country on the Arabian Peninsula, a nation state.

clue.text: Becoming active again, finally striker offside: Spain moving up

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of each of the three words

parts.note: an ascent is a movement upwards

explanation.surface: A striker is flagged offside at the end while Spain climb the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' takes the last letters of striker, offside and Spain: R, E, N.
explanation.definitionFit: Renascent means being reborn, reviving or showing renewed vigour.
